title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, runbooks, and team wiki
author: Ava Martinez
content:
Overview
========
This document is the canonical reference for the Serving Runtime team: architecture overview, kernel-scheduling policies, profiling playbooks, benchmarking harness, release notes, known issues, incident/runbook procedures, and team wiki pointers. It is intended for engineers operating or extending the runtime and on-call SREs.

Summary of contents
-------------------
- Runtime architecture and component responsibilities
- Kernel scheduling design and policy (fairness, preemption, slot sizing)
- Profiling playbook: how to profile a production regression and required artifacts
- Benchmarking suite: workloads, commands, thresholds, and result format
- Release notes (latest) and upgrade guidance
- Known issues and recommended mitigations
- Runbooks and incident response checklists
- Team wiki pointers and ownership

Runtime architecture (high level)
--------------------------------
Short intro: The runtime is a microservice architecture optimized for low-latency token generation and high throughput for batching workloads. Primary service components:

- api-gateway (service: rwd-api): validates requests, authenticates, rate-limits, returns streaming responses.
- request-router (service: rwd-router): routes requests by policy (latency, cost, region, model-compatibility).
- coordinator (service: rwd-coordinator): groups compatible requests into batches, maintains per-request metadata and KV-cache lookups.
- batch-worker / model-worker (service: rwd-worker): executes model inference on GPU(s) using model-driver and kernel-selection library.
- kv-cache (service: rwd-kvcache): prefix/KV cache store (in-memory + Redis backing) to accelerate repeated prompts.
- model-driver (library: rwd-kernels): encapsulates kernel selection, quantized paths, and execution primitives (CUDA kernels / Triton or JIT).
- telemetry-agent (service: rwd-telemetry): collects traces, metrics, and profiled artifacts to S3/nsys store.

- rwd-api: owner "frontend" team (contact: @frontend-oncall)
- rwd-router: owner "routing" (contact: Elias Chen)

SLOs and performance targets
- Short responses (<= 32 tokens output, small prompt): p50 < 80ms, p95 < 250ms, p99 < 500ms
- Medium responses (<= 256 tokens): p50 < 250ms, p95 < 700ms, p99 < 1.2s
- Throughput: baseline throughput per A100-80GB-like instance: 1,200 tokens/sec for gpt-like medium models at batching target.
- Success rate: 99.95% of requests must return a response or known error code within 30s.

Alert thresholds
- Alert if p95 latency increases by >25% from baseline for 10m window.
- Alert if GPU utilization falls below 15% or >95% for sustained 5m window (investigate).
- Alert on error rate >0.5% for 5m.

Kernel scheduling: design and operational policy
------------------------------------------------
Goals: minimize tail latency, maximize GPU utilization, and provide tenant fairness across workloads.

Key concepts
- Slots: a slot is a scheduling unit representing a batch-capacity on a GPU. Slots are sized by estimated memory and compute requirements.
- Preemption: lightweight preemption is supported between sequence length boundaries to prioritize low-latency queries.
- Kernel classes: fast-attention kernels (small seq), general-attention (long context), quantized-int8 kernels.
- Affinity: model shards are pinned to specific GPUs where possible to keep KV cache warm.

Scheduling policies (implemented in rwd-scheduler)
1) Latency-first queue for short requests: requests tagged as latency-sensitive (by route/config) enter a high-priority queue and are scheduled with minimal packing.
2) Throughput queue for batchable requests: best-effort requests accumulate up to batch-size or time-window (default 8ms) then dispatched.
3) Fair-share weight per-customer: each customer has a token-weight that influences slot allocation under contention.
4) Preemption window: if a high-priority request waits >5ms in queue and would improve p99 by preempting a batch-start, scheduler will preempt if resulting cost < configured threshold (default 1.5x single request cost).

Operational knobs (config keys)
- scheduler.batch_time_ms (default 8)
- scheduler.max_batch_tokens (default 4096)
- scheduler.preemption_enabled (default true)
- scheduler.latency_priority_timeout_ms (default 5)
- scheduler.fairness_decay_half_life_s (default 300)

Kernel selection and execution
- The model-driver runs a heuristic to pick kernel implementations based on: model type, sequence length, quantization profile, and available CUDA capability.
- Kernel fallbacks: if optimized kernel fails, fallback to safe-generic kernel and emit metric rwd.kernel.fallback with error code.

Profiling playbook: how to triage a production perf regression
------------------------------------------------------------
Purpose: give a repeatable process for collecting the correct artifacts and making a remediation plan.

Required artifacts (for an oncall ticket)
- Cloud trace id (X-Trace) linking frontend -> worker (must be included in the alert).
- nsys capture (recommended) or NVTX timeline of the affected request on the worker. Save to S3 with path: s3://rwd-profiles/{date}/{trace-id}.nsys
- rwd-metrics snapshot: 2m window of prometheus metrics around incident (prometheus query IDs or csv).
- Worker logs (rwd-worker) +/- 1m around trace id.
- Kernel fallback/error counters and GPU utilization metrics.

Steps to collect artifacts (SRE oncall)
1) Identify a representative trace: use the alerting trace id.
2) Run a short nsys capture on a replica of the worker in staging with the same model, batch size and sequence length:

   ```bash
   # start capture for 10s (staging replica)
   sudo nsys profile --output /tmp/{trace-id}.qdrep --sample=none --capture-range=nvtx --trace=nvtx,cuda --processes=all --stop-on-exit --timeout=10s 
   # convert to timeline (optional)
   nsys stats /tmp/{trace-id}.qdrep --report gputrace > /tmp/{trace-id}.timeline.txt
   ```

3) Annotate timeline with the rwd-trace id using NVTX markers (production code uses rwd-telemetry NVTX helpers).
4) Upload artifacts to s3 and link them to the incident ticket.
5) Compare kernel invocations (fast-attn vs general-attn), memory copies (H2D/D2H), and kernel durations.

Heuristics for common regressions
- Symptom: p99 latency regression + high kernel fallback rate -> likely a kernel selector bug; check rwd.kernels.selector.* logs and recent changes.
- Symptom: high GPU memcpy overhead -> mis-sized batch or unexpected large context; check batch token size and kvcache misses.
- Symptom: sudden drop in throughput with high utilization -> kernel thrash (too many small kernels); consider increasing scheduler.batch_time_ms by 2-5ms as quick mitigation.

Benchmarking suite: running consistent perf comparisons
------------------------------------------------------
Location: repo infra/benchmarks/serving-harness (contact: performance-eng)

Benchmark types and canonical workloads
- micro-bench: single-request latency for 8/32/128 tokens output on representative models (gpt-medium, code-small)
- macro-bench: sustained throughput with mixed request sizes and distributions (production-like traffic replay)
- quant-bench: quantized model perf for int8/qat profiles

Result format
- CSV (per-run) with columns: run_id, model, instance_type, batch_time_ms, batch_size, tokens_per_sec, p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, kernel_fallbacks, kvcache_hit_rate

How to run (example)

```bash
# run micro-bench against staging service
cd infra/benchmarks/serving-harness
python run_bench.py --model gpt-medium --instance a100-80gb --scenario micro --out results/micro-gpt-medium.csv --seed 20260220
```

Acceptance thresholds (example)
- micro-bench p95 <= 250ms for short-response scenario.
- throughput bench: tokens_per_sec >= baseline - 10% for new releases.
- quant-bench: output quality drift measured by eval harness must be <= 2% degradation in accuracy metrics.

Benchmarking CI integration
- PRs touching rwd-kernels must run a subset of the micro-bench in CI (fast smoke) and upload results to the artifacts bucket. A full macro-bench is required for kernel changes that touch scheduling or memory paths.

Release notes (latest significant runtime release)
------------------------------------------------
Release: serving-runtime v1.8.0 (2026-02-20)
Highlights:
- Scheduler: added latency-priority queue and preemption improvements to reduce p99 for short requests by ~15%.
- Kernel selector: new heuristic for long-context models that reduces fallback rate by 40%.
- KV cache: added async prefetch for pinned-shards to reduce cold-start latency.
- Observability: NVTX markers enriched with span ids to simplify timeline correlation.

Upgrade guidance:
1) Roll workers by model-family groups (small/medium/long-context) to warm KV caches.
2) Increase rollout window to 30m and monitor p99 and kernel.fallback metrics.
3) If p99 increases >10% in canary cohort, rollback immediately using standard release rollback (see runbook).

Known issues (summary and workarounds)
------------------------------------
- ISSUE-2026-001: Occasional kernel selector NPE for model variants with missing config. Workaround: set legacy-kernel-fallback=true and restart worker. Fix: PR #1422 merged (scheduled full rollout 2026-03-01).
- ISSUE-2026-007: High memcpy overhead when kvcache hit_rate < 10% for long-context workloads. Workaround: temporarily increase scheduler.batch_time_ms to 12ms and enable kv-prefetch for pinned shards.
- ISSUE-2026-013: Rare race causing request-router to hold stale model-compat caches after model rollback. Workaround: flush rwd-router cache with CLI: `rwd-routerctl flush-cache --model <model-id>` and restart router.

Runtime runbooks and incident response
-------------------------------------
Incident: p99 latency regression detected on production for model X
Priority: P1 if customer impact > 5% requests or key customer SLA triggers

Immediate checklist (0-10 minutes)
1) Acknowledge pager and create incident ticket; include alert trace id.
2) Collect summary metrics (prometheus dashboards: serving-runtime/default) and the trace.
3) Identify whether regression is isolated to a model-family or global.
4) If isolated to one model-family, start targeted canary routing to alternate model variant using rwd-router feature-flags.

10-30 minutes: mitigation and rollback
1) If mitigation is not found quickly, rollback the most recent runtime workers in affected region:
   a) Use k8s rollout undo for rwd-worker deployment group: `kubectl -n serving rollout undo deployment/rwd-worker-{group}`
   b) Monitor p99 for 10m; if stable, proceed with controlled roll forward.
2) If resource exhaustion (GPU mem) is observed, scale out worker pool by +20% via autoscaler or temporarily increase instance type.

Post-incident (30m-72h)
1) Capture full telemetry and profiling artifacts and link them to postmortem.
2) Run targeted micro-bench with the failing model variant and compare to last-known-good results.
3) Produce RCA and assigned action items with owners and deadlines (see incident postmortem template).

Common CLI and diagnostic commands
- Check scheduler queue sizes:
  `rwd-ctl scheduler status --json`
- Flush KV cache for model shard:
  `rwd-kvcachectl flush --model <model-id> --shard <shard-id>`
- Trigger a single-request repro in staging with tracing enabled:
  `python infra/benchmarks/repro.py --model <model> --input-file repro/payload.json --trace-id <ticket-id>`

Appendix: quick reference tables
-------------------------------
Scheduler config defaults:
| key | default | description |
| scheduler.batch_time_ms | 8 | time window to accumulate batch (ms) |
| scheduler.max_batch_tokens | 4096 | max tokens per batch |
| scheduler.preemption_enabled | true | allow preemption of in-flight batches |

Common metrics to inspect (prometheus)
- rwd_request_latency_seconds{quantile}
- rwd_gpu_utilization_seconds_total
- rwd_kernel_fallback_total{kernel,code}
